title: Ukraine Struck Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant VZPP-S on 22 June. Gusev Confirmed Damage; the Russian MoD Did Not Name the Plant in Its Overnight Summary. The Components Fed Three of Russia's Consequential Weapon Systems — and the Production Equipment Depends on Western OEM Support Sanctions Already Block (22 June 2026)
narrative:
On 22 June 2026, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine struck the Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant (VZPP-S, also known as 'Sborka') using 'high-precision, air-launched cruise missiles.' The strike hit around 11:40 local time per Voronezh Oblast Governor Alexander Gusev, set the main production building ablaze, and produced multiple distinct fires visible in geo-located videos from Exilenova+, Supernova+, and ASTRA. Gusev confirmed 'significant damage' and acknowledged 'casualties, including some in critical condition,' declaring a state of emergency in the surrounding district.

VZPP-S is legally divided into VZPP-Mikron and VZPP-S. It has been under U.S. sanctions. Its components feed three of Russia's most consequential weapon systems. The Kh-101 air-launched cruise missile uses VZPP transistor assemblies for the UVK-208 navigation/control unit, including the 1NT2514 NPN transistors and the 2TS622A arrays. The Iskander-K's 9M727 / R-500 cruise missile uses semiconductor arrays for the Zarya-61M onboard digital computer. The Pantsir-S1 air-defense system uses diodes and transistor assemblies for the TVK-2 television guidance channel on the 72V6 combat vehicle. Defence Express notes that the plant 'housed highly specialized production equipment that is extremely sensitive to vibration and even to the concentration of dust particles in the air,' making the cruise-missile-plus-fire combination 'highly unlikely that production can be restored in the foreseeable future.'

The Russian framing is the credibility story. Gusev's official Telegram statement said 'air defence forces had destroyed several high-speed targets in the skies over Voronezh' without specifying the precise target of the strike. The Ministry of Defence's overnight summary, per ASTRA, did not enumerate a successful interception over Voronezh at all — it reported interceptions elsewhere, but skipped Voronezh. Russian channels monitoring the strike claimed three Storm Shadow missiles were shot down over the city in addition to those that hit the plant. Even if that claim is accurate, the Russian MoD's choice to enumerate only interceptions while not naming the targeted facility is the canonical pattern of acknowledging the tactical win (the intercept) while eliding the strategic loss (a sanctioned microelectronics plant on fire).

The Voronezh strike is the third leg of a coordinated multi-day Ukrainian campaign. On 20 June, Ukrainian drones struck the Tyumen refinery at approximately 2,000 km into Russia. On 21 June, Ukrainian missiles struck the Kerch oil depot and Kavkaz port, producing a 47-km smoke plume per Crimean Wind. On 22 June, the VZPP-S strike. FIRMS satellite thermal anomalies have also been recorded at the Tavriiska Thermal Power Plant (470 MW), TES fuel/gas storage, and gas distribution stations across occupied Crimea; S-300/S-400 positions were ablaze on Cape Zyuk on 21 June. Russian refinery utilization is now approximately 20% below pre-war levels per The Deep Dive and UNITED24 Media.

Storm Shadow attribution is plausible but unconfirmed by Ukraine. Russian channels and some military bloggers suggested British-supplied Storm Shadow / SCALP cruise missiles were used. The Deep Dive notes that Russia destroyed another microelectronics manufacturer, Kremniy El in Bryansk, with Storm Shadow on 10 March 2026 — a precedent pattern that Defence Express cites for the Voronezh attribution. Ukraine has not confirmed the weapon type, leaving the attribution in the same evidentiary position as the Russian MoD's silence: both sides have not said what they could have said.

analysis:
The Voronezh strike is a documentary-credibility piece about a sanctioned weapons-component supply-chain node, not an OSINT satellite story. The pattern that makes it distinct from the Tyumen refinery strike of 20 June or the Moscow refinery Pantsir-friendly-fire incident of 18–19 June is the production-equipment dependency: VZPP-S did not only assemble transistors, it operated Western-made production equipment that requires calibration and repair support Russia cannot legally obtain under existing sanctions.

Gusev's official statement is a tell. He confirmed 'significant damage' and 'casualties, including some in critical condition' — that is unusually direct acknowledgement for a Russian regional governor speaking about a sanctioned microelectronics facility hit by Ukrainian cruise missiles. He did not, however, name the facility. The Russian MoD's overnight summary skipped Voronezh entirely, while enumerating interceptions elsewhere. This is the asymmetry: the Russian side acknowledges damage and casualties (because the fires are independently video-documented) and acknowledges interceptions (because Storm Shadow shootdowns are testable against open-source fire patterns), but declines to name the sanctioned facility because naming it confirms the supply-chain pedigree to a Western sanctions-enforcement audience.

The 1NT2514 and 2TS622A specificity is what makes this story a sanctions story, not a strike story. Defence Express's identification of the exact transistor part numbers feeding the Kh-101's UVK-208 navigation unit, the Zarya-61M computer on the 9M727 / R-500 cruise missile, and the TVK-2 television guidance channel on the Pantsir-S1 is the kind of specificity that lets Western sanctions officers verify supply-chain participation. The U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control can cross-reference the part numbers against export-control records; the European Union can update its sanctions list to include additional named persons at VZPP-S; the UK Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation can add named parent-company entities. None of this requires classified intelligence.

The production-equipment dependency is the load-bearing finding. Defence Express's note that VZPP-S 'traditionally relies heavily on foreign-made equipment from leading Western manufacturers' is the structural reason this strike is more strategically significant than its physical footprint suggests. Routine calibration is 'already difficult under sanctions'; repairs are 'even more problematic.' The combination of physical damage (fire at the main production building) and contamination (the plant's sensitivity to dust and vibration) means that even partial production resumption would require either (a) Western OEM support that sanctions prohibit, or (b) sanctions-evasion procurement through third countries (China, Turkey, UAE, Kazakhstan) at substantially higher cost and lead time.

The triple-strike campaign context (Tyumen → Kerch/Kavkaz → Voronezh) confirms that this is a coordinated Ukrainian doctrine of hitting Russian energy and weapons-component infrastructure in rapid sequence. The Voronezh strike is the supply-chain leg of that campaign — the leg whose downstream effects propagate into Kh-101 production rates, R-500 / 9M727 production rates, and Pantsir-S1 spare-parts availability, all of which are observable in the open-source battlefield-fingerprint layer.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: On 22 June 2026, Ukrainian cruise missiles struck Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant (VZPP-S) and set the main production building ablaze. Voronezh Governor Alexander Gusev acknowledged 'significant damage' and 'casualties, including some in critical condition' and declared a state of emergency. The Russian Ministry of Defence's overnight summary did not name the targeted facility, despite enumerating interceptions elsewhere. The strike destroyed a sanctioned U.S.-designated microelectronics facility whose components feed three named Russian weapon systems: the Kh-101 (UVK-208 navigation unit with 1NT2514 transistors), the Iskander-K / 9M727 / R-500 (Zarya-61M computer arrays), and the Pantsir-S1 (TVK-2 television guidance diodes). The production equipment VZPP-S operated depends on Western OEM support that sanctions already block; the combination of fire damage and contamination sensitivity means production resumption requires either prohibited Western service or sanctions-evasion procurement at substantially higher cost and lead time. Independent OSINT groups (Exilenova+, Supernova+, ASTRA) and independent Russian-émigré outlets (Novaya Gazeta Europe, The Moscow Times) geo-located the strike and identified the facility from open-source footage; resident video showed sequential cruise-missile impacts along the length of the main production building — the visual signature of a coordinated multi-missile strike, not a single point of impact. The Voronezh strike is the supply-chain leg of a coordinated June 20–22 Ukrainian campaign that included Tyumen refinery (~2,000 km deep strike), Kerch oil depot and Kavkaz port (47-km smoke plume per Crimean Wind), and S-300/S-400 positions on Cape Zyuk in occupied Crimea.
